title: About
text: Record linkage is often taught as either pure method or pure software. This project keeps both in view: short theory pages explain the decision points, and longer R scripts show how those decisions play out in reproducible workflows.

title: About
text:
Scope
Examples are written with public health and epidemiology in mind, but the same patterns apply to other linkage problems: cleaning noisy identifiers, reducing candidate pairs, comparing records consistently, and documenting uncertainty.

title: About
text:
Design choices

Theory first, applications second.
Synthetic person-level health data where real public data would be inappropriate.
Real public datasets where organisation, place, or registry examples fit the task.
Frozen Quarto outputs so GitHub Pages deployment does not need R in CI.

title: Evaluate linkage quality
text:
Precision asks how many accepted links are correct. Recall asks how many true links were recovered. Which matters more depends on the analytic goal.

true_positive <- 92
false_positive <- 8
false_negative <- 15
precision <- true_positive / (true_positive + false_positive)
recall <- true_positive / (true_positive + false_negative)
round(c(precision = precision, recall = recall), 3)

precision    recall 
     0.92      0.86

title: Evaluate linkage quality
text:
Bias in downstream estimates
False non-matches can remove events unevenly across subgroups. False matches can misclassify outcomes or inflate denominators. Report linkage quality with the analysis, not as a disconnected appendix.

title: Evaluate linkage quality
text:
Sensitivity analysis
Vary thresholds, re-run key estimates, and describe how sensitive conclusions are to plausible linkage error.

title: Compare fields systematically
text: Names and addresses usually need graded comparison rather than exact equality. String distances help identify near matches, while agreement patterns across several fields describe how much evidence points toward a true link.

title: Compare fields systematically
text: Names and addresses usually need graded comparison rather than exact equality. String distances help identify near matches, while agreement patterns across several fields describe how much evidence points toward a true link.

title: Compare fields systematically
text:
Fellegi-Sunter logic
Fellegi-Sunter scoring contrasts the chance of observing an agreement among true matches (m) with the chance of observing it among non-matches (u). Rare fields with high agreement often carry more weight than common fields.

title: Compare fields systematically
text:
EM in practice
Expectation-maximisation is often used to estimate m and u probabilities when labelled matches are unavailable. It does not remove the need for judgement; it just makes the weighting step more systematic.

title: Why link records?
text: Record linkage brings together records that refer to the same person, event, organisation, or place when there is no single perfect key. In epidemiology, this often means combining cohort, hospital, registry, and mortality data to answer a question that no one source can answer alone.

title: Why link records?
text: Record linkage brings together records that refer to the same person, event, organisation, or place when there is no single perfect key. In epidemiology, this often means combining cohort, hospital, registry, and mortality data to answer a question that no one source can answer alone.

title: Why link records?
text:
Deterministic and probabilistic linkage
Deterministic linkage uses exact or rule-based agreement on selected fields. Probabilistic linkage allows disagreement and weighs evidence across multiple identifiers. Most real workflows mix the two: exact agreement where identifiers are strong, probabilistic scoring where they are not.

title: Why link records?
section: Where linkage sits in an analytic pipeline
text:
Where linkage sits in an analytic pipeline
Linkage is upstream of analysis but downstream of data acquisition, governance, and cleaning. Errors introduced here carry forward into denominators, follow-up time, exposure histories, and outcome ascertainment.

title: Theory
text: Theory pages are short by design: one concept each, concrete headings, and only enough R to clarify a point. Read them in order if you are new to linkage, or use the sidebar to jump to the step you need.

Who this is for
This site is for analysts, researchers, and data stewards who need a practical linkage workflow in R: clear preprocessing, transparent matching rules, and reporting that is good enough for audit, reproducibility, and epidemiologic interpretation.

title: Report what you did
text: Use GUILD and RECORD guidance to describe data sources, identifiers, blocking, comparison, decision rules, quality checks, and any clerical review.

title: Report what you did
text: Use GUILD and RECORD guidance to describe data sources, identifiers, blocking, comparison, decision rules, quality checks, and any clerical review.

title: Report what you did
text:
What to document

data custodians and legal basis
source population and date coverage
identifiers used, transformed, or excluded
blocking passes and comparison fields
thresholds, review rules, and final match counts
how linkage error was assessed and discussed







NoteReporting note



A reviewer should be able to understand the linkage design, its limits, and its likely effect on estimates without reverse-engineering code.

title: Report what you did
text:
Privacy and governance
Linkage design should respect the separation principle wherever possible. Privacy-preserving linkage methods can reduce direct exposure to identifiers, but they still need clear evaluation and governance.

title: Turn scores into decisions
text: After scoring candidate pairs, decide which scores mean accept, reject, or review. A single threshold is simple but often too blunt for operational work.

title: Turn scores into decisions
text: After scoring candidate pairs, decide which scores mean accept, reject, or review. A single threshold is simple but often too blunt for operational work.

title: Turn scores into decisions
text:
Clerical review
A review band is useful when the cost of a false match is high and some ambiguous pairs can be inspected. The review process should be documented, reproducible, and ideally blinded to downstream outcomes.

title: Turn scores into decisions
text:
One-to-one and many-to-many constraints
Entity resolution rules matter. A death record may link to one person, but a household address may validly link to many people. Constraining all problems to one-to-one can create artificial errors.

title: Prepare identifiers well
text: Common linkage fields include names, dates of birth, sex, addresses, postcodes, and administrative IDs. Each behaves differently: names vary in spelling, dates transpose easily, and addresses often change over time.

title: Prepare identifiers well
text: Common linkage fields include names, dates of birth, sex, addresses, postcodes, and administrative IDs. Each behaves differently: names vary in spelling, dates transpose easily, and addresses often change over time.

title: Prepare identifiers well
text:
Standardisation steps

normalise case and whitespace
strip punctuation that is not informative
split compound fields consistently
encode missingness explicitly rather than silently dropping records
preserve raw values for audit and reruns







WarningPitfall



If you overwrite raw identifiers during cleaning, you lose the ability to inspect disagreement patterns later.

title: Prepare identifiers well
text:
Missingness and encoding
Missingness is part of linkage information. A blank date of birth is different from an impossible date, and both are different again from a parse failure caused by encoding.

title: Block before you compare
text: Comparing every record in file A to every record in file B is usually infeasible. Blocking reduces the candidate set by requiring coarse agreement on a few fields before detailed comparison.

title: Block before you compare
text: Comparing every record in file A to every record in file B is usually infeasible. Blocking reduces the candidate set by requiring coarse agreement on a few fields before detailed comparison.

title: Block before you compare
text:
Common strategies
Use stable, fairly complete fields for blocks: year of birth, sex, postcode prefix, or a phonetic name key. Multi-pass blocking is often safer than a single narrow rule.

title: Block before you compare
section: The cost of blocks that are too tight
text:
The cost of blocks that are too tight
If a true match fails the block, it never reaches the scoring stage.

people_a <- 1000
people_b <- 1000
full_pairs <- people_a * people_b
blocked_pairs <- people_a * 8
c(full_pairs = full_pairs, blocked_pairs = blocked_pairs)

   full_pairs blocked_pairs 
        1e+06         8e+03 


A good block cuts the search space sharply without discarding plausible matches.
